demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Arun, at eighty years old, moves through his small, quiet house with the practiced economy of a man long accustomed to solitude. It has been five years since his wife, Meera, passed away, but the true hollowing out of his world began decades earlier, on a churning grey sea off the Oregon coast. For forty years, he served in the Coast Guard, a source of immense pride that now feels like a brand of shame. He cannot deliberately recall the full sequence of that day; when he tries, his mind meets a strange, resistant fog. Instead, the memory lives in him as a series of disconnected, violent snapshots. The shriek of the winch cable under strain, the icy sting of salt spray hitting his face, the sickening, hollow thud against the hull, and the wail of the medevac siren that seemed to cut right through the storm's roar. When these fragments ambush him, they are not memories but a full sensory assault. He is back on the deck of the cutter, the vessel lurching beneath his feet, the freezing rain soaking his uniform, the metallic taste of fear in his mouth.

In the immediate aftermath, Arun developed a set of silent rules for managing the intrusion. He learned to sense the approach of a memory and would immediately try to push it from his mind, a mental shove that left him breathless. If that failed, he would tell himself a story: it was a chaotic rescue, a freak wave was to blame, the event was not as bad as the fragments made it seem. When the guilt still clawed at him, he would force himself to think only of positive things-Meera's smile, the birth of his son, the taste of a perfect mango-a desperate and exhausting act of will. He had come to believe the event was not a tragic accident but a direct result of his own personal failing. A better man, a more vigilant guardsman, would have anticipated the swell. The incident happened, he was certain, because of the sort of person he was: fundamentally defective. This belief became the lens through which he saw the world, a place of hidden dangers he was ill-equipped to handle.

This pervasive sense of threat dictates the geography of his life. His son has tried to get him to join a senior group at a new community center, but Arun refuses. He avoids any unfamiliar place where he cannot immediately assess the risks and identify all the exits. Even in his own home, he occupies only one chair: a worn armchair in the corner of the living room, which offers a clear view of both the front door and the hallway. From this post, he remains on constant guard. Yet, this vigilance coexists with a strange recklessness. Some evenings, he takes long walks after dusk, striding along uneven sidewalks without a flashlight, a part of him almost daring a fall. It is a quiet form of risk-taking, a way of tempting a fate he feels he probably deserves.

His triggers are woven into the fabric of daily life. An ambulance screaming past his street can leave him trembling for an hour, the sound yanking a sensory fragment of the failed rescue into the present moment. His son's attempts to get him to visit a coastal state park are met with sharp, uncharacteristic anger; the sight of waves crashing against rocks is unbearable, a direct portal to his greatest failure. Even discussions about the future feel perilous. When his granddaughter recently spoke excitedly about her plans for college, Arun felt a wave of panic and nausea. He could not connect with her hopefulness; it felt like a language he was no longer permitted to speak. He abruptly changed the subject, leaving her looking confused and hurt. It was the look on her face that finally broke through his defenses. He saw his private torment was no longer private; it was now casting a shadow on the people he loved most. Arun has come to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a fragile wish to stop being a source of pain for his family, terrified that the defectiveness he feels within himself is, and always will be, irreparable.
